prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Whoever, Fire, Not

outputs.L1:
Whoever first brought wood and coal  
To start the fire did his part well;  
Not all wood catches from a match,  
Nor coal from wood before it has burned to charcoal.  

The wood and coal in question caught flame  
And flared beautifully, touching the air—  
That air which takes a flame from anything.  
Somehow, the fire was furnaced;  
And then the time was ripe for some to say,  
“Proper banking of the furnace saves the coal.”  

I have seen them set to work, each in his way,  
Though all with shovels and with ashes,  
Never resting until the fire seemed nearly dead;  
Whereupon they would crawl, in hooded nightcaps,  
Contentedly to bed.  

Sometimes, left alone, the fire would die;  
But just as often, spiced tongues,  
Remaining by the hardest on until day, would flicker up—  
Never strongly, but enough for anyone who cared to rake for them.  
Yet roaring fires have never been made that way.  

I should like to tell those people that one grand flare,  
Transferred to the memory tissues of the air,  
Is worth as much—or, for dull minds that reckon in gold,  
More than all the money ever saved by banking coal.
outputs.L2:
Whoever first carried in the wood and coal  
To get the blaze begun did a worthy job.  
Not every stick will catch from a single match,  
And coal will not easily burn from wood  
Until the wood has first become charcoal.  

But this particular fuel did ignite,  
And it rose in a splendid flare, reaching into the air—  
That air which can take fire from almost anything.  
In some way the blaze became a furnace,  
And soon the moment came for certain people to declare,  
“Banking the furnace properly conserves the coal.”  

I have watched them go at it, each according to his method,  
All using shovels, all using ashes,  
Working on until the fire looked nearly extinguished;  
After that, satisfied, they would creep off  
In their hooded nightcaps to bed.  

At times, when left by itself, the fire  
Would simply go out; yet just as often,  
A few sharp tongues of flame, clinging longest to the hardest fuel,  
Would last until morning and flicker up again—  
Not powerfully, but enough for anyone willing to stir them.  

Still, great roaring fires have never been created in that fashion.  
I would like to tell such people that a single magnificent blaze,  
Once passed into the remembered fabric of the air,  
Is worth as much as—or, to blunt minds that measure value in gold,  
More than—all the money ever kept  
By saving coal through careful banking.
outputs.L3:
The poem praises the person who first discovered how to kindle fire successfully with wood and coal. That figure is celebrated as a kind of benefactor, someone who gave humanity not merely warmth, but beauty, comfort, and a powerful source of life. Once the wood and coal properly catch, the fire grows into a strong and splendid blaze. It becomes something vivid and almost glorious, filling the room with light and heat.

The poem then contrasts this admiration for a full, living fire with the cautious habits of people who are mainly concerned with saving fuel. Such people try to conserve coal by banking the fire with ashes, covering it over so that it will last longer and burn more slowly. In moderation, this may seem practical, but the poem criticizes excessive restraint. When too many ashes are piled on, the fire is smothered rather than preserved. By morning, instead of finding a bright or useful flame, one may discover only a dull, weakened ember, nearly dead.

Through this contrast, the speaker reveals a clear preference. The value of fire lies not simply in how long it can be made to last or how much money can be saved by using less coal. Rather, its true worth is found in the greatness of its blaze—in its warmth, brilliance, and unforgettable power while it burns. For the speaker, one magnificent and memorable fire is worth more than all the fuel conserved by caution or thrift. The poem therefore becomes a celebration of intensity, generosity, and fullness of life over mere economy and restraint.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores the conflict between saving one’s resources and spending them in a moment of full, vivid intensity. It begins with the practical image of people banking a furnace with ashes in order to keep the fire alive while using as little coal as possible. This act represents caution, thrift, and the desire to make warmth last by controlling and limiting the flame. The fire is not allowed to burn freely; it is covered, restrained, and preserved for future use.

Against this careful habit, the poem sets a different value: the beauty and power of a fire that is allowed to blaze. A banked fire may endure longer, but it gives less light, less heat, and less wonder. A great flame, even if it consumes its fuel quickly, creates an experience that is intense, memorable, and alive. The poem suggests that there are moments when it is better to spend energy fully than to hoard it timidly.

By the end, the speaker favors the single brilliant blaze over cautious preservation. The poem is not merely about coal or fire; it is also about how to live. It implies that a life devoted only to saving, conserving, and avoiding loss may miss the very experiences that give life meaning. Beauty, passion, and intensity may be brief, but their value can exceed that of mere endurance. The poem therefore celebrates the memorable brightness of a fully burning fire and suggests that one magnificent moment can be worth more than a long period of careful restraint.
outputs.L5:
Whoever stands too close to the fire must learn to respect its heat. It can warm a cold room, light the darkest path, and bring people together in moments of need. But fire is not something to treat carelessly. It demands attention, patience, and responsibility.

Whoever uses fire wisely understands its power. It is not only a force of destruction, but also a symbol of hope, courage, and renewal. From a small candle to a great flame, fire reminds us that even a little light can push back the darkness.

Still, fire is not always easy to control. It can grow quickly, changing from comfort to danger in a moment. That is why people must handle it with care and never forget its strength. Whoever learns this lesson will see fire not as an enemy, but as a powerful force that must be respected.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Robert Frost–style blank verse poem using the metaphor of banking a coal fire to criticize people who stifle passion or creativity in the name of prudence.
counterfactuals.output:
They say the sensible man banks his fire  
Before he climbs the narrow stairs to bed,  
Draws ash across the coals with careful hands,  
And leaves no red eye open to the dark.  

I’ve seen such hearths at morning, gray and cold,  
The chimney holding back its bit of sky,  
The kettle dull, the room gone hard with frost,  
While all the household praises having saved.  

Saved what? A stick or two of honest flame,  
A little heat that might have warmed the night,  
A flare that might have startled someone’s dream  
And sent him down to mend the world with song.  

There is a thrift that spends the soul by halves,  
A caution colder than the risk it fears.  
It calls the spark a danger, breath a waste,  
And lays its shovel gently on the heart.  

Better the crackle, better one bright log  
That takes, and in the taking gives itself,  
Than all the prudent ashes men preserve  
To prove no house of theirs was ever burned.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem in an early 20th-century New England voice about wood, coal, furnaces, and the idea that one bright blaze is worth more than all the fuel saved.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Bright Blaze**

I have known men to count the sticks of wood  
As if each birch-bolt had a soul in pawn,  
And shake the coal down softly, like a sin,  
Lest morning find the cellar-bin too low.  
They kept a house so prudent of its heat  
The windows wore their frost inside, like ferns,  
And children learned to breathe with mittens on.

Yet I have seen, upon a bitter night,  
One armful brought in reckless from the shed,  
One shovel more of anthracite let fall,  
And then the furnace answer like a beast  
That had been starved but had not yet forgot  
The old red language of the heart of things.

How quick the parlor loosened at the seams.  
The clock resumed its tick. The kettle sang.  
The lamplight seemed less lonely on the wall.  
A woman’s hand came out from under wool;  
An old man told the story to the end;  
The boy beside the register grew brave  
And planned a ship, a farm, a railroad line.

What is a winter saved, if saved too well?  
What profit in a cellar full of cold?  
Wood is but forest waiting to be flame,  
And coal, black daylight borrowed from the earth.  
Spend it, I say, when darkness has the room.  
Let one bright blaze go roaring up the flue—  
There’s more kept safe in that than all we spare.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a pastiche of Robert Frost’s “The Bonfire,” but make it about tending a furnace and the folly of dampening a fire too much.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Furnace**

I had a furnace in the cellar wall,  
A little sun shut up in brick and iron,  
And, coming down at midnight with the pail,  
I found it breathing low, but breathing on.  

The house above had settled into frost;  
The windows wore their ferns the wrong side in.  
I shook the grate and heard the cinders fall  
Like sleet among dead leaves along a road.  

Then, thinking how a fire must not run wild,  
I turned the draft down tighter than was wise,  
And shut the dampers with a careful hand,  
As if all prudence lay in starving flame.  

The blue tongue faltered. What had leaped lay still.  
A red eye blinked beneath a lid of ash.  
The warmth drew back into itself and sulked,  
And all the cellar gathered up its cold.  

There is a thrift that loses what it saves,  
A caution that can freeze the very thing  
It means to shelter from too much desire.  
A fire, like heart or house, must have its air.  

So I went back and gave the chimney leave,  
Opened the draft and broke the crust apart.  
The coal took hold again, first one small star,  
Then many, answering in a darkened sky.  

Above, the pipes began their knocking talk;  
The rooms remembered what the walls were for.  
I stood there, warm-faced, wiser by a chill:  
You do not keep a fire by keeping it down.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary poem that begins with someone bringing the first wood and coal to start a fire, then reflects philosophically on how cautious people bank the coals until the fire nearly dies.
counterfactuals.output:
He brought the first wood in, and coal in a blackened pail,  
as if he carried night itself indoors  
to teach it how to shine. The room was cold;  
the windows held their breath. He knelt, arranged  
the splintered sticks, the dull ancestral stones,  
and struck one match—small flare of faith,  
brief flower opening in his hands.

Then flame took root. It climbed the wood,  
found resin, found the hidden summer  
sealed in every ring, and loosened it to gold.  
The coal blushed slowly, like an ancient thought  
remembering its origin in fern and sun,  
and all of us drew nearer, palms outstretched,  
our faces gathered from the dark.

But those who fear the hunger of a blaze  
soon come with iron tongs and prudent eyes.  
They speak of thrift, of danger, of the night  
that must be metered hour by hour. They rake  
the living brightness inward, heap gray ash  
over the red heart, whispering, Preserve.  
And so the fire, saved too carefully, declines.

How often is the soul thus kept—  
not spent, not lost, but guarded into dimness;  
its ardor hidden for some later need  
that never comes. We call it wisdom, sometimes,  
to shelter what was meant to leap and sing,  
until the hearth gives off no heat, no light,  
only a sullen pulse beneath the dust,  
a nearly vanished star we crouch beside,  
hands folded, saying: See, it still endures.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a free-verse/blank-verse poem with irregular rhymes about a fire being started, people trying to preserve it with ashes, and the speaker concluding that a single grand flare matters more than thrift.
counterfactuals.output:
They coaxed the first spark out of splinters,  
bent close, as if listening for a name.  
The dark held its breath around them.  
Then orange climbed the twigs—  
a small flag, a living blade, a room of heat  
opening in the cold.

All night they guarded it with careful hands,  
feeding it little, saving what would burn.  
When the flame sank, they banked it under ash,  
gray blankets over a restless heart,  
whispering, Keep. Endure.  
Do not spend yourself.

By dawn the pit was pale and mean,  
a thrift of embers, a miser’s red  
hidden beneath the powder of yesterday.  
They stirred and begged it back,  
cupped smoke like water,  
praised the art of lasting.

But I had seen the first blaze leap—  
how it made every face suddenly true,  
how shadows fled like thieves from gold,  
how even the stones seemed briefly crowned.

Let the ashes teach their narrow lesson.  
Let careful hands count fuel and years.  
I would choose the upward roar,  
the great unhidden flare,  
one sovereign burst against the dark,  
over a lifetime saved in dust.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
